Interviewer: This is a United States Holocaust Memorial Museum volunteer collection interview with Peter Miller, conducted by Jack Smith on August 6th, 2007, in Silver Spring, Maryland. This is tape number one, side A. What is your full name? Your full name, your name at birth.
Interviewee: That — that’s it.
Interviewer: It —
Interviewee: My full name is Peter Miller.
Interviewer: Do you have a middle name?
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: No. And that is the name you were born with?
Interviewee: That’s right.
Interviewer: And where were you born?
Interviewee: In Koblenz, Germany.
Interviewer: And your date of birth?
Interviewee: January 26, 1922.
Interviewer: Let’s talk about your family, who — the members of your family. Tell me about your parents.
Interviewee: My — my fa — my — my parents are very — very ha — very well — big on my number — on my number of people. The-They wonderful people, they were — they were very good to me as a student. I went to a — a *** which is a — German for a high school where — where was whole lot of *** months afterwards. Anyway — but my parents took care of me all the time.
Interviewer: What were your parents’ names?
Interviewee: Max, call Maxime Max, and A-Alice Miller.
Interviewer: Mm-hm. And where was your father born?
Interviewee: In Kirchberg. Is there — a picture there of a si — on the steep — on the stoops, sitting there with the children. He was born in a little town in Koblenz which is a — on — what, 40 miles north of Ko-Koblenz.
Interviewer: And your mother’s name?
Interviewee: Davids, her last name dav — dav —
Interviewer: And her — her first — her first name?
Interviewee: Oh, alee — Alice Miller, or di-di — her name was Davids before.
Interviewer: Mm-hm. And where was she born?
Interviewee: In a little town along the Mosel in Budek, which — well, which is *** little town, and still is little town.
Interviewer: Mm-hm. And how did they meet?
Interviewee: Don’t know.
Interviewer: And when — th-then they got married, they met each other, what does your father do? What kind of work did your father do?
Interviewee: My father — th-the earliest I can tell you about, that he worked with machines. He manufactured machines, including weighing machines for — for bars and grills, and weight — weight machines for people to get weighed on. And he traveled in — in the area of Koblenz within — within 50 miles, I would say. And he — he was also a wounded li — a wa — a war veteran, as a German soldier, where his hand was completely crippled and he could — he would not drive. That’s about the only thing, he did everything else, but he was not be able to drive. And he was a very *** person. He made a family wa — very wonderful and close, and he ma — made us *** my mother was a — a very correct lady. She had to go to her vacations like the German women did, and my father made sure that she got to the right places. It was a very nice family, and we had enough money to live in the very nice areas in — in Koblenz.
Interviewer: What street did you live on, do you remember?
Interviewee: What street?
Interviewer: Do you remember the address?
Interviewee: Yeah. I’m — wa — what I left, this was Koblenz, that’s from a — my father’s house. This is his house. I saw — I could draw another pictures of it after it was ruined by the dri — American dri — bombers.
Interviewer: What street was your house on?
Interviewee: Kleerstrasser. Kleerstasser 74.
Interviewer: Mm-hm.
Interviewee: And there was a *** there’s two, one, two, and he owned it with a fellow by the name of Richel, who is another Jewish fellow, who own — owned the cigar store. So together they did a very nice — had a — had a very nice life. But *** you know — you know the ending.
Interviewer: Yeah, we’ll get to that. We’ll get to that. Do you have — I mean — a brother? Did you have a brother?
Interviewee: I have a brother who is four years younger.
Interviewer: And his name?
Interviewee: Ernest.
Interviewer: Ernest. So let’s — was the neighborhood a mixed neighborhood of Jews and non-Jews? It must have been if his — that Mr. Richel was —
Interviewee: I wouldn’t say Jews ***. I don’t think it was a very important thing at the time, and I remember.
Interviewer: Mm-hm, mm-hm.
Interviewee: It was a neighborhood which would — had businesses and par — apartments at the same time. It was still a small — it’s a small town. So the — the — the neighborhood, it cul — it cul — accu — got accustomed to the *** who lived there and the people who work there. Very calm neighborhood.
Interviewer: Did you have a large extended family, aunts and uncles or grandparents nearby?
Interviewee: My father had three brothers and a sister, which lived not in Koblenz. They lived in co — in Düsseldorf. And my — my mother had a brother who lived in Koblenz who was in the wine business and he so — he was probably — he came over to this country as a refugee. His wife was not a Jewish woman, who was a Christian woman, but a very good one. A wonderful wom-woman, wonderful to us, and we were very close. They live here in Broadway in New York.
Interviewer: Mm-hm.
Interviewee: And we had good times.
Interviewer: How — how religious was your family? Were they observant?
Interviewee: Pardon me?
Interviewer: How religious was your family? Were they a very observant Jewish family?
Interviewee: I don’t know what you mean.
Interviewer: Did your family — it was a Jewish family, did you observe any Jewish holidays?
Interviewee: Oh yes. We — we — in — generally we were Jewish people. We feel very, very Jewish, all this.
Interviewer: Did — did you belong to a synagogue?
Interviewee: As a — as a young fellow, I — I belonged to a yel — yeah, a — a — a youth group. Not a *** a religious one, but a youth group from — formed by the chur — by the — by the — the temple.
Interviewer: So your family belonged to a temple?
Interviewee: Mm. No. Only me, sometimes.
Interviewer: And did you observe Passover, or any of the holidays? Passover, or Hanukkah? Did you observe any of those holidays at home?
Interviewee: Did I do any holi — da — what?
Interviewer: Did you observe any of the Jewish holidays at home?
Interviewee: Yes. I observed the time where you had to *** ma-matzel, we did. And some of the holidays, yes. It — it — it was — it was forced on — onto us by — by — by politics, to be closer to — to your — to your religion than you really were.
Interviewer: Was your family a Zionist family? Were your parents Zionists?
Interviewee: What? Are they what?
Interviewer: Were your f — parents Zionists?
Interviewee: Zionists?
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: No. They were American at — they were German people who lived in Germany, very happily and loved this country.
Interviewer: How many generations back did your family live in Germany, do you know?
Interviewee: How far — when do they come from someplace else, you mean? I think they came from Spain, but my knowledge is as — very limited. I don’t think I would — can comment on it any further. That maybe the great-grandfather came from Spain.
Interviewer: Now, growing up you went to public school?
Interviewee: Yes, I went to —
Interviewer: You went as a little boy, as a little boy you went to public school with Jewish —
Interviewee: Public school for four years.
Interviewer: Yeah, with Jewish and non-Jewish children?
Interviewee: Together, mixture.
Interviewer: Uh-huh.
Interviewee: There was no — no difference.
Interviewer: And any anti-Semitism?
Interviewee: None. Very little. I don’t remember se — se — anti-Semitism from any one of my je — friends in the class —
Interviewer: Uh-huh.
Interviewee: — until of — ca — became a Hitler neighborhood —
Interviewer: Right.
Interviewee: — you know, a political neighborhood.
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: Then of course it changed completely.
